plain: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1, Public Law 119-21) was signed July 4, 2025. It extended and added federal tax cuts and cut spending on Medicaid and food assistance. The question is whether passing it was right.
agree_means: Agreeing means backing the law’s lower federal taxes and its new rules for Medicaid and food assistance, and accepting its cost to the deficit.
disagree_means: Disagreeing means opposing it over its deficit cost, its Medicaid and food-assistance changes, or its hit to Colorado’s budget.

now.text: The law made the 2017 tax cuts permanent and added more. The standard deduction for joint filers is $31,500 and the child tax credit is $2,200. It added deductions for tips and overtime. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) says it adds $3.4 trillion to deficits over 2025 to 2034, against its January 2025 baseline.

now.text: States must make Medicaid expansion adults ages 19 to 64 show 80 hours a month of work or school, and recheck eligibility every six months.

sources.title: Health Provisions in the 2025 Federal Budget Reconciliation Law (KFF)
sources.quote: Requires states to condition Medicaid eligibility for individuals ages 19-64 applying for coverage or enrolled through the ACA expansion group (or a waiver) on working or participating in qualifying activities for at least 80 hours per month or attending school at least half-time.

sources.title: Health Provisions in the 2025 Federal Budget Reconciliation Law (KFF)
sources.quote: Requires states to conduct eligibility redeterminations every 6 months for Medicaid expansion adults.

now.text: Colorado’s income tax follows federal changes at once. State analysts estimated a $1.2 billion revenue loss in 2025-26 and a true budget gap of $680 million to $783 million. An August 2025 special session closed corporate tax breaks (about $250 million), used $325 million of reserves and cut spending.

stakes.text: Nationally, the Tax Policy Center finds the average household saves about $2,900 in 2026: about $150 in the lowest fifth (up to $34,600) and $12,540 in the top fifth ($217,101 and up). The Colorado Fiscal Institute, a progressive think tank, estimates Coloradans earning over $863,000 save nearly $70,000 and the bottom 20 percent $130.

case_against.text: Gov. Jared Polis, a Democrat, says the law cuts health care and food access and “slashed the state budget” with corporate tax breaks.

research_notes: The Chrome extension was not connected, so I read the CBO pages in the built-in Claude Browser pane in my own tab (CBO returned 403 to scripted fetches): publications 61570, 61367, 61837, 61738 and the interactive distribution tool. Those sources carry via: browser. The decile figures come from the interactive tool's table, which may be script-rendered; CBO offers the same data as a CSV. Axios and CPR pages returned 403 and I did not cite them. For a reviewer: (1) The $1.2 billion revenue loss is an August 2025 estimate. The June 2026 forecast shows individual income tax collections far above forecast and corporate collections down, so the net cost is uncertain. (2) The '>150K lose coverage' figure is a July 2025 state presentation citing a consulting-firm estimate (the slide spells it 'Mannat'); 377,000 is the expansion population exposed to the rules, not a loss estimate. (3) SNAP: the 10.09 percent FY2025 rate is from the USDA table; the 15 percent tier is from the state human services slide, which says the share uses the FFY25 or FFY26 rate. The CDHS director's July 2025 estimate used the FFY24 rate (9.97 percent, 10 percent tier). I did not compute a dollar cost. (4) Rep. Evans' tax claims are from his May 2025 release on the House-passed version; Rep. Crank's is from his July 3 final-vote release. (5) Tax Policy Center figures are national (July 2025) and come through CBS News because I could not read the TPC site. The Colorado Fiscal Institute's Colorado figures come through Post Independent and are CFI's own estimate. (6) The vote list is from the governor's office (partisan source, factual list). (7) CBO's $3.4 trillion is against its January 2025 baseline, in which the 2017 cuts expire; a current-policy baseline gives a different number that I did not fetch. (8) The web search budget ran out before I could find a Colorado-specific neutral estimate of household tax savings.
